query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

In this context, one of the biggest challenges is the development of structural and functional materials that can withstand the conditions inside the reactor: high temperature, high heat flux, and intense flux of high energy neutrons []. The diverter, located at the bottom of the plasma chamber, where the thermal power from the plasma is exhausted [], is one of the most challenging areas. Tungsten (W), with a high melting temperature, low sputtering rates, low neutron activation, and low tritium and deuterium retention [,], was chosen as the plasma-facing material. CuCrZr alloy was chosen as the heat sink due to its high thermal conductivity and strength. However, there is a gap between the operating temperatures of these two materials. Tungsten presents a high ductile–brittle temperature transition (DBTT) [], which requires a high-temperature operation, while CuCrZr alloy presents relatively low working temperatures (180–350 °C) [], with loss of ductility caused by irradiation embrittlement at lower temperatures and loss of mechanical strength at higher temperatures due to over-aging [,]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. Multi-component refractory elements-based alloys possess a mainly BCC structure. One of the most interesting HEA types is a system with coherent BCC and B2 phases with a microstructure similar to Ni-based alloys. The difference is that the disordered BCC phase is present as cubic nanoparticles. This structure provides a combination of high strength and high plasticity at high temperatures and is standard for Al-containing multi-component alloys. Thus, for the AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr alloy, its yield strength is 745 MPa at 1000 °C, and good plasticity is preserved (the height decrease is >50% under compression) []. However, there can also be observed oxides and intermetallic phases, such as Laves phases, in the refractory HEAs that can affect the materials’ ductility. For example, in the NbCrMoTaTiZr, CrNbTiZr, and CrNbTiVZr alloys, the Laves phase is formed in the BCC-matrix because of the smaller radius of Cr in comparison to other elements [,,]. Nevertheless, in Reference [], an NbMoTaWVCr alloy with an extremely high yield strength of 3416 MPa and good plasticity of 5.3% at room temperature was obtained. decision.trend: The trend in the research is to explore the effects of different elements on the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). Earlier studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Recent studies have focused on the effects of specific elements, such as Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr, on the mechanical properties of HEAs and MEAs.

This is based on earlier studies that reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, and the successful use of Mo in other HEAs and MEAs.
